news.content_original: News Sports Ticket Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWS Florida dengue cases surge to 296, largest US outbreak in decades State adds 44 more cases C. A. Bridges Cheryl McCloud USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Oct. 9, 2026, 10:44 a.m. ET Florida has reported 296 locally acquired dengue fever cases this year, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The majority of cases, 259, have been confirmed in Hillsborough County, where one death has been reported. Several counties have declared states of emergency to expedite mosquito control, with 16 counties under a mosquito-borne illness alert or advisory. Florida reported 44 new locally acquired cases of dengue fever in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health. The disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes. That brings the statewide total to 296 for the year as of Oct. 3, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous highest number of Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases for the year. Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents The bulk of the cases have been in Hillsborough County, which has 259 confirmed cases, while other locally acquired cases have been reported in seven other counties. Broward County reported its first confirmed human dengue case on Oct. 5. One death was confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of “dengue infection” along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. The previous largest outbreak was in Hawaii's Big Island, where 264 local cases were reported in the six months between September 2015 and March 2016. Florida's surge began three months ago. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection Three Tampa Bay-area counties — Pasco, Hillsborough, and Pinellas — have declared states of emergency to expedite mosquito control operations and cut through paperwork for emergency response. Currently, 16 counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. West Nile virus and chikungunya — which are also transmitted by mosquitoes — have also been reported in Florida this year, but in far fewer numbers than dengue. Another human case of West Nile was reported in Holmes County in the period of Sept. 27 - Oct. 3, bringing the state total to seven for the year. No new chikungunya cases were reported. ➤ Dengue cases keep climbing in Florida. This is how to protect yourself There have also been 262 dengue cases associated with international travel reported in Florida this year, 215 of which were from travel from Cuba, according to the FDOH. Most of the cases were reported in Miami-Dade County. Although these cases were not locally acquired, mosquitoes that bite infected people in the state can transmit the disease to others. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. Dengue still surging in Florida. See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Oct. 3, there have been 296 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in seven counties, which is up from 252 reported Oct. 1. There have also been seven positive samples of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 296 cases 259 in Hillsborough County 20 in Pinellas County 8 in Miami-Dade County 3 in Orange County 3 in Pasco County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: 7 cases 2 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County (1 an asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 case 1 in Miami-Dade County What's causing the Florida outbreak of dengue fever? One reason for the surge in dengue cases is due to a comibation of "climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. Those factors include warmer temperatures, increased rainfall and standing water, and human travel from other countries with outbreaks. Health data show that 215 of the 262 Florida cases acquired from outside the country were people who had recently traveled from Cuba. Most of the cases were DENV-2, one of the disease's four serotypes and the serotype behind Cuba's current epidemic, where fuel shortages are hampering fumigation efforts, according to Forbes. 16 mosquito-borne illness alerts, advisories issued for these Florida counties A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Brevard Broward Holmes Leon Manatee Martin Palm Beach Polk Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." All Florida residents could take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. C.A. analysis_zh.event: 佛罗里达州今年报告了296例本地获得性登革热病例,标志着美国数十年来最大的暴发。佛罗里达州卫生部确认希尔斯伯勒县有一例因登革热感染、败血性休克和多器官衰竭导致的死亡。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 已报告296例本地获得性登革热病例,其中259例在希尔斯伯勒县。确认有一例死亡。此外,还报告了262例与国际旅行相关的登革热病例,其中215例来自古巴。此次暴发促使16个县发布蚊媒疾病警报或建议。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 多个县已宣布紧急状态以加快蚊虫控制工作。佛罗里达州卫生部继续与当地蚊虫控制合作伙伴协调,开展针对性的应对措施。此次暴发被归因于气候和人为因素,包括气温升高、降雨量增加以及来自其他登革热暴发国家的人类旅行。

supplementary_news.title: Mosquito Hotspots in a Brazilian Slum Reveal Where Chikungunya Risk Concentrates
supplementary_news.excerpt: A high-resolution study in Salvador, Brazil, links Aedes aegypti breeding hotspots and chikungunya seropositivity to unpaved yards, garbage accumulation, and household vulnerability.
supplementary_news.rss_summary_html: A high-resolution study in Salvador, Brazil, links Aedes aegypti breeding hotspots and chikungunya seropositivity to unpaved yards, garbage accumulation, and household vulnerability.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, October 12, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Mosquito Hotspots in a Brazilian Slum Reveal Where Chikungunya Risk Concentrates by October 12, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Mosquito Hotspots in a Brazilian Slum Reveal Where Chikungunya Risk Concentrates Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In the crowded informal settlements of Salvador, Brazil, the risk of catching chikungunya is not spread evenly from street to street. It clusters around unpaved yards, piles of garbage, and the shaded peridomestic spaces where the yellow fever mosquito, Aedes aegypti, finds ideal conditions to breed. A new high-resolution study published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases has mapped these fine-scale vulnerabilities with unusual precision, combining mosquito egg counts, household surveys, serological testing, and Bayesian spatial statistics to reveal exactly where the virus finds its footholds in one low-income community. The research, led by Jaqueline S. Cruz, Hussein Khalil, and colleagues working with long-standing infectious disease programs in Salvador, set out to answer a deceptively simple question: which socioeconomic and environmental factors determine both where Aedes aegypti mosquitoes flourish and which residents show evidence of past chikungunya virus infection? To do so, the team spent months embedded in a vulnerable informal community, deploying ovitraps and drawing blood samples from residents between October 2021 and June 2022. The result is one of the most granular portraits yet of how urban poverty, ecology, and viral transmission intersect at the scale of individual households. Chikungunya virus, or CHIKV, is an arbovirus transmitted primarily by Aedes mosquitoes, the same vectors responsible for dengue and Zika. First identified in Tanzania in the 1950s, the virus has swept through tropical and subtropical regions in successive waves, causing explosive epidemics characterized by fever and often debilitating joint pain that can persist for months or years. In Brazil, incidence has risen sharply in recent years, with the burden falling disproportionately on socioeconomically marginalized neighborhoods where irregular water supply, poor waste collection, and unpaved surfaces create abundant breeding habitat. Despite this clear ecological logic, the microscale drivers of transmission within informal settlements have remained poorly quantified, largely because most surveillance operates at municipal or district levels too coarse to capture household-level heterogeneity. To overcome this limitation, the researchers combined two complementary strands of evidence. The first was entomological: 194 ovitraps, simple containers holding water and a wooden paddle where female Aedes aegypti deposit their eggs, were distributed across the study area and monitored regularly. Egg counts per trap served as a proxy for vector abundance, capturing the spatial texture of mosquito proliferation at resolutions far finer than conventional indices. The second was serological: the team enrolled 888 residents aged five years and older, collecting blood samples to test for antibodies against chikungunya virus, alongside detailed questionnaires covering sociodemographic characteristics, housing conditions, and environmental exposures. Analyzing these data required statistical machinery capable of handling both spatial autocorrelation and multiple sources of uncertainty. The team employed Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation, or INLA, a Bayesian computational framework well suited to spatial modeling, to fit models linking ovitrap egg counts and individual seropositivity to their candidate predictors. Because the models report credible intervals rather than single point estimates, the findings convey a calibrated picture of how confident one can be in each association, an important safeguard when working with complex, noisy community data. The entomological results were striking. Ovitraps placed in peridomicile locations, the spaces immediately surrounding homes such as yards and alleys, recorded substantially higher egg counts than traps in other settings, with an incidence rate ratio of 1.99 and a 95 percent credible interval spanning 1.31 to 3.06. In other words, simply being near a house nearly doubled the expected mosquito egg density, implicating the shaded, cluttered, and water-holding niches around dwellings as primary breeding grounds. Households reporting food insecurity, a marker of deep socioeconomic deprivation, also showed higher egg counts around their properties, as did homes with unpaved yards and locations surrounded by greater garbage density, which carried a risk elevation of 25 percent per unit increase. The serological analysis told a parallel story about human exposure. Among the 888 participants, several factors were independently associated with testing positive for chikungunya antibodies. Elderly residents faced roughly double the odds of seropositivity compared with younger adults, a pattern consistent with cumulative lifetime exposure and possibly with reduced access to protective behaviors such as air conditioning or intact window screens. Housing quality emerged as a powerful signal: living in a home with uncovered brick walls, a hallmark of unfinished informal construction, doubled the odds of prior infection, while having a yard, whether paved or unpaved, was associated with twofold to nearly threefold increases in seropositivity. Residents who reported personally seeing mosquitoes in or around their homes showed 94 percent higher odds of seropositivity, suggesting that individual perception tracks real exposure reasonably well. Intriguingly, the model also incorporated remotely sensed satellite data, specifically Land Surface Temperature, and the spatially smoothed ovitrap egg counts as continuous covariates of seropositivity. Both variables showed positive associations with point estimates that did not exclude the null in the credible intervals, but their inclusion demonstrates a methodological advance: temperature measured from orbit at microscale resolution, and local mosquito abundance itself, can be layered into risk models alongside household characteristics. Warmer microclimates accelerate mosquito development and viral replication, and the authors argue that such fine-scale thermal variation deserves attention in future control planning, particularly as urban heat islands intensify. Taken together, the findings paint a coherent picture of chikungunya risk as a product of converging vulnerabilities. The same environmental degradations that concentrate mosquito breeding, unpaved ground, accumulated refuse, and precarious construction, also coincide with the socioeconomic conditions, food insecurity, elderly residents, and unfinished housing, that heighten human exposure. Crucially, the spatial overlap between ovitrap hotspots and seropositive clusters suggests that where mosquitoes are most abundant, residents are indeed being infected, validating ovitraps as a cheap and actionable surveillance tool that could direct interventions before outbreaks ignite. The authors conclude that effective chikungunya control in informal settlements cannot rely on generic campaigns alone. Instead, strategies must be tailored to the neighborhood scale: upgrading basic urban infrastructure, clearing garbage, paving and managing yards, targeting breeding sites around homes where egg densities peak, engaging communities in mosquito-source reduction, and incorporating microscale temperature data into risk maps. In an era of expanding arboviral threats across the tropics, this study offers a blueprint for precision public health, showing that with careful spatial epidemiology, the invisible geography of risk in a vulnerable community can be made visible, and ultimately, actionable.
